explain.say: A rich duke draws back a curtain to show a visitor a painting of his late wife, and he talks, and talks, until we realise something terrible. Robert Browning published My Last Duchess in 1842. The panels follow the Duke's speech, moment by moment.

explain.say: What is a dramatic monologue? Sort the parts on the board: one speaker who is not the poet, at a dramatic moment; a silent listener we only guess at; and a speaker who reveals more than he means. Here the listener is an envoy arranging the Duke's next marriage. Can you spot a line where the Duke gives himself away?

Look at the panels. The Duke complains that his wife smiled at everyone and thanked people for small favours as warmly as for his ancient name. He would not stoop to tell her. Then he says he gave commands, and all her smiles stopped together. What do you think those commands were?

explain.say: This is dramatic irony: we understand more than the speaker does. On the left, what the Duke says; on the right, what we hear. Browning writes in rhyming couplets, but runs sentences over the line ends, called enjambment, so it sounds like real talk. Why hide the rhymes?

Browning wrote many of these. In Porphyria's Lover a man kills his lover to keep one perfect moment, and The Ring and the Book tells a Roman murder trial voice by voice. A gentle note: several of his speakers are violent men. Brilliant work. Challenge: write six lines as a villain who believes he is the hero.

faq.a: A poem spoken by one character, not the poet, to a silent listener at a key moment, in which the speaker reveals their character, often more than they intend. Browning and Tennyson made it a major Victorian form.

faq.q: Did the Duke kill his wife in My Last Duchess?
faq.a: The poem only says he gave commands and her smiles stopped, so it hints rather than states. Browning is reported to have said the commands were that she be put to death, or perhaps shut in a convent.

faq.q: Who is the Duke talking to?
faq.a: An envoy from a count whose daughter the Duke plans to marry next. So the speech is also a warning about how the new wife must behave, and it ends with talk of her dowry.
asks: Who is the listener in My Last Duchess?

faq.a: Browning's 1836 monologue in which a man strangles his lover with her own hair to preserve a moment when she seemed wholly his, then sits calmly with her body. It is a study of a disturbed, possessive mind.
When a sentence runs on from one line of poetry to the next without a pause. In My Last Duchess it hides the rhymes and makes the Duke sound like he is really talking.

facts: My Last Duchess was published in 1842 in Browning's collection Dramatic Lyrics.
It is usually linked to Alfonso II d'Este, Duke of Ferrara, whose young wife Lucrezia de' Medici died in 1561.
The poem is 56 lines of rhyming couplets in iambic pentameter.
